title: Errors as Values and the ? Operator
goal: A Result carries the error to the caller. The ? operator does it in one character.

sections.text: Operations that can fail return `Result<T, E>`: either `Ok(value)` or `Err(error)`. Like `Option`, the failure is part of the type. Unlike `Option`, the error side carries information about what went wrong, for example a `ParseIntError`.

sections.caption: ? forwards the error and keeps the happy path flat.

sections.text: The `?` operator does one thing: if the value is `Err`, return it from the current function immediately. If it is `Ok`, take the value out and continue. One character replaces a whole `match`, and the function's signature stays honest.

Two habits look similar and are worse. `.unwrap()` turns a bad input into a panic. `.unwrap_or(0)` hides the failure inside a normal-looking value, so the caller cannot tell garbage from a real zero. When the signature already declares an error type, `?` is the tool that keeps the promise.

explanation: Result carries the error as a value. Use ? to propagate it; avoid unwrap_or defaults that hide failures.
